paras: The shooting of Charles Parker was the fatal wounding of an Adirondack guide by a constable in northern New York in August 1881, after Parker had been accused of assaulting a woman he was guiding and hunted by guides who threatened to lynch him. Parker escaped from custody, was shot by Constable Cole while being retaken at Long Lake, and died at Forked Lake days later. The case drew wide notice because the woman, Mrs. George Bull of Philadelphia, was bound for Senator Platt's camp, and because accounts of the shooting divided.

According to a Troy dispatch of July 27, Parker, a guide at Blue Mountain Lake, was taking Mrs. Bull "yesterday" from Forked Lake to Long Lake, where she was to stay with ex-Senator Platt. A Watertown dispatch described him as a resident of Elizabethtown who "was not a regular guide" and resented the established guides.

The Troy dispatch charged that Parker made "a heinous assault" on Mrs. Bull, nearly strangling her, and a later dispatch called it an attempted rape. By the account of W. F. Hall, given to the Albany Argus, it happened on the last carry between the two lakes, and Parker then forced her silence under threat of drowning. When the boat landed at the Platt camp, Hall seized it and called for the camp guides to hold Parker, but he jumped ashore, took his rifle from his own camp and gained a two-hour start.

The wire reports said the guides were "looking for Parker and threaten to lynch him," sworn to have him "dead or alive." The Watertown dispatch put the searchers at one hundred, all armed, who "would have shot him at sight." A July 29 dispatch had him arrested at Kingston, Ontario, Hall called that man only "supposed to be Parker," and the Watertown dispatch of August 2 placed him in the Essex County Jail at Elizabethtown.

An Albany dispatch said Parker then escaped from Constable Cole's custody and that Cole arranged a meeting at the foot of Long Lake, "promising, as alleged, not to arrest" him. Parker came by boat with his wife on a Friday morning; when he pulled back toward shore and reached for his gun, Cole fired once with a Winchester rifle, shattering his left arm and wounding him in the breast. His deputy, Kelly, swam to the drifting boat and helped take the wounded man.

Parker died at Forked Lake early on a Tuesday morning after giving an ante-mortem statement, according to the Troy Times. Anger then turned on the constable: "threats against Cole are heard on every hand," the Albany dispatch reported, and the guides who had threatened to lynch Parker were said to be "now highly incensed." No report of an inquest or of any proceeding against Cole appears in the coverage.

The story moved as a Troy wire dispatch on July 28, headed "An Indecent Assault by an Adirondack Guide" in Portland, and was followed on July 30 by "The Adirondack Ravisher Captured." White papers treated Parker's guilt as settled, calling him "the villain" and "a bold, bad man," and repeated the guides' threats without criticism. The Meriden Republican defended Adirondack guides "as a class" and hoped the culprit would receive "the severest penalty that the law inflicts."

The Towanda Daily Review reprinted the Philadelphia Press's account of George Bull, a Democratic party chairman, learning the news at breakfast. After the death the Troy Times reported that "sympathy is about equally divided," though one informant confined Parker's support to "the less reputable portion" of the community. None of the reports states Parker's race or presents the case in racial terms.

A Troy dispatch of August 9 said Cole caught Parker "early this morning" near Ausable Lake, while the Albany account, repeated in Washington and Wilmington, placed the shooting on a Friday morning at Long Lake. The Troy Times said Parker lay thirty hours uncared for and that a message offering his surrender on conditions had been sent to Senator Platt before the shooting, but added that he had reportedly said he "would not be taken alive." Reports also differed on Mrs. Bull's host, naming ex-Senator Platt of New York, Thomas C. Platt, or Senator Platt of Connecticut.

reader.title: Shooting of Charles Parker
bases: The only violence done was Constable Cole's shooting of Parker while retaking him after an escape from custody (A16, A17, A19); the guides' threats to lynch him (A1, A2, A11) were not carried out.

Parker died of a single rifle shot fired by Constable Cole, with only his deputy Kelly beside him, while retaking an escaped prisoner (A16, A18, A20); the armed guides who had threatened to lynch him are not reported to have caught or harmed him (A1, A11). Whether Cole broke a promised truce was alleged but not established (A16, A18).

The accusation and the guides' hunt come from a Troy wire (A2), a Watertown dispatch (A11) and W. F. Hall's account in the Albany Argus (A14), and the shooting and death from separate Troy (A15, A18) and Albany (A16) dispatches, though details of the shooting differ.

accounts.label: Troy dispatch of Aug. 9
accounts.gist: Cole caught Parker near Ausable Lake early on Aug. 9 after a desperate encounter, shooting him near the heart.

accounts.label: Troy Times (Parker's side)
accounts.gist: Reports that Cole broke a truce, that Parker lay thirty hours uncared for, and that he was meant to escape; offset by reports that he vowed not to be taken alive.

framing.detail: Headlines such as 'An Indecent Assault by an Adirondack Guide' reported the guides' vow of vengeance without comment.
The Meriden Republican defended guides 'as a class' and called for 'the severest penalty that the law inflicts'.
The Watertown dispatch called Parker 'a bold, bad man' and 'the fiend' and explained the guides' armed search as 'the wrath of the guides'.
After the death the Troy Times aired 'two sides to the main story' while noting 'the better class' condemned Parker.
